text:
It is nice that you are happy with the update.

The internal all-around LED lighting "...which you'll notice, especially as you are driving..." sounds like a drawback. I don't want a distraction in the car as I am driving at night.

Deletion of the stalks was definitely a bad move.

That dashboard fabric has got to go. Aftermarket wood will hopefully be available.

The rear display screen is pointless. I have zero interest in back seat passengers being entertained.

As you got low by the headlights, it has circles in the front bumper, so hopefully that isn't an emergency hood release and is Tesla keeping that spot available for ultrasonic sensors once it sinks in that deleting those was a mistake.

Anyway, for me, it seems like the best plan is to go with a 2022 or pre-Highland 2023. Then, after some of these refreshes get into accidents, buy the doors from a salvage yard to have the double-glazed windows. Thus, getting the one important improvement and not sacrificing any of the good things.

Just a shame Tesla cookie-cutter manufactures these. If we had a menu to select the things we like from the pre-Highland version and add what we like feom post-Highland and delete what we don't like from post-Highland,....then we would be truly custom ordering our car.

text:
I own a 2019 and 2023 Model 3. Recently, a kid hit my 2019 with his truck, so I have been able to enjoy a rental Audi A5 Sportback. 

I was very excited to drive a comparable German sports sedan. The Audi I think is around $55K, so more expensive. And the Audi is only 100lbs lighter. It's got a nice interior. 

But the Model 3 is a far, far sportier car. Compared to the Audi, the Tesla has got direct steering feel. Its handling is flat, neutral, and completely controllable. Throttle response is instant, and has enough power to deliver whatever you need to do. 

The Audi is awkward. You step on the gas pedal, and you wait a second as it feels like it's bogged down, then without warning, the turbo kicks in for angry acceleration, even if you don't want it. In the most "dynamic" setting, the car is numb, and it reminds me of my 1981 Buick Regal I had in high school. You'll never upset the chassis in the Audi because it's so underpowered. And, it's no fun to drive. 

To add insult: I can't figure out how to refuel the Audi from my house. I have to stop at gas stations. 

I can't wait to get my 2019 Model 3 back from the shop...

text:
oh no, blinkers as buttons is a v bad idea. There were where they were in most cars because it was practical to turn the steering wheel and on the way just nudge the stalk in a direction the wheel is turning with your finger. It was obvious and intuitive. With buttons you need to remember that right is up, left is down, and if the wheel is already turned 90 deg anticlockwise (on a roundabout for example), suddenly right blinker is the button on the left. How does that make any sense? Not to mention that you don't just turn the wheel holding your hands in the same spot, you kinda always default into holding the wheel more or less on the same level, in the middle. Meaning, at 90 deg, the buttons are at the bottom of the steering wheel, and you need to reach down to them (and figure out that the right blinker is on the left actually lol). I get that this wasn't a consideration in the US because you guys have like 10 roundabouts in total, but in EU and basically anywhere else they are everywhere, in different sizes, different angles of exit etc, so muscle memory won't help here, and IMO, even if it did, it still seems dangerous or inconvinient at best.

This is objectively, the worst design choice in a car I've seen in a while. And I don't understand why they did it to begin with. I see 0 benefits. If it was for minimalism, I can't see how a button in front of you is more minimalistic than a thing sticking out behind the wheel that you can't see for most of the time, because, well, its behind the wheel :D
Just innovation for the sake of innovation. The worst kind.

Thankfully in EU this won't be allowed (right?)

Also, where is the horn button? I don't see anything in the middle... is it in the menus or what happened? (that was btw already played around with in Renault cars from around 2010s. Everyone hated that they moved the horn from the middle, to a stalk in front of the blinkers. Why? Who knows, they are french, nobody understands them anyway).

PS. Great vid as always Marques!

Speed and acceleration is fun in a fast gas car. I’ve driven a plaid and a model 3 performance. Both those cars are incredibly quick, but the thrill is not the same compared to a gasoline engine, putting down those numbers.
It’s like cooking a steak, you could put that steak in a microwave to cook it and cook it quick. Or you could put that steak on a grill and it’ll take longer to cook, but it’ll taste a lot better and it’s more fun to grill. At the end of the day you end up with two cooked steaks.

text:
Yeah!!! The embargo is lifted and we can see this car...Finally! I must add that you missed perhaps THE most exciting thing about this car = The new adaptive suspension. Usually there's a tradeoff dilemma for engineers - to make it daily/liveable, meaning too soft for sporty driving or race car harsh wherein potholes, heaves, asphalt patches, expansion joints and speedbumps jar your 
teeth. All the best cars from Germany any and even Cadillac ( MRC or Magnetic Ride Control ) offer adaptive damping that assesses road conditions, speed and turning force to provide accurate compliance for the situation at hand. This system is automatic or user configurable as well, so have at it as you please. Track mode v.3 is an upgrade too with new tweaks. The new wheels are lighter, too.

The suspension has new geometry and the brake pads , while not carbon ceramic, are new and improved over the last gen Performance 3. It would be nice, Elon, to have some new, differentiating colors other than the same six choices you've offered for the last 6 years as seen on millions of other Teslas. 

The seats look amazing yet I agree those steering wheel buttons need to have a tactile click. Its not a deal-breaker for me, but no stalks and no gear shifter are weird. I know there's Auto Drive like in the Plaid and people say it works well, so maybe that would make up for that omission...to me.

The Ioniq5N is a wagon and the looks don't do it for me. Its also slower and over $70,000.. The fake transmission and phoney engine noises are controversial. In my brain, when manufacturers create fake engine noises for EVs ( hello Porsche ) they lose me. Its like fake news - Intellectually, I know it's BS. Some OEMs cut the gears slightly different in their sporty EVs which creates a true, mechanical sound that is pleasing and communicates sensations of speedier motation.

All-in, I'm stoked to drive it and may trade in my 2018 Long Range. Next comes the price. If it's signicantly less than a Hyundai N or BMW, it'll be a no-brainer. Being the most American car you can buy also helps. A new S Plaid still tops $90,000 with wheels and paint. Maybe a used Plaid? Love the hatch but its a big car.....

Thank you for making this video and I hope you can give it a go on the track soon!

It’s relatively much cheaper now than when I got mine, which makes it much less exclusive, rare or desirable to me.

GM have completely nailed it and with supercharger network access now too, it was absolutely the right move for me.  Very happy with something higher end, rarer, more luxurious and people across the board stop me to rave about this vehicle.  GM did an incredible job with the Hummer EV, and it bodes well for their next gen EV’s elsewhere in the company.

text:
And if that bothers you that much, you can likely get an 18 inch aftermarket wheel for it to regain some if not most of that range back.

But in my experience with my Model Y, long distance travel has gotten a lot easier overall in a Tesla because they keep adding more and more superchargers in many places, so going as far as you absolutely can on one charge is less of an issue than how fast can you charge at each station you do stop at.

Or as Out of Spec Motoring calls it, "supercharger hopping". While you do have to stop more often, your overall trip is usually faster because you're spending less time at said superchargers compared to doing long deep charges at fewer ones that the car tends to do if you don't want to optimize the trip speed.

At one stop, it told me to deep charge for about 40 minutes to make it to the next supercharger which was about two hours away. If I was eating at a restaurant, that might've been fine. But since it was the middle of the night, I instead picked the next supercharger in between where I was charging and where the car wanted me to go. I only had to charge another 5 minutes to make it to the next one, then stopped at that one for maybe 15 minutes, compared to if I did the 40 minutes it originally wanted me to do.

This doesn't always work of course, because if the supercharger is full or you're at a V1/V2 supercharger, you'll probably have to wait. Should also be interesting as more non-Tesla EVs are able to use the V3/V4 superchargers and how they'll impact Tesla owners.

Needless to say, he is massively underwater on his car loan. Teslas experienced abnormal depreciation rates due to a double whammy: Tesla repeatedly raised prices throughout 2021 and into 2022, meaning they had to reduce prices throughout 2023. Then, federal tax credit was reintroduced to 3/Y. IMO, Model 3 had no business starting at $47k *before* taxes and fees. The depreciation that we recently saw won’t be seen again for a long time. It sucks that cars from various brands experienced massive depreciation over the past 2 years or so, causing many people to be underwater on their loans. But that should teach people not to bite off more than they can chew. At the end of the day, cars are depreciating assets, not investments. Either buy with cash, or put down at least 35% before getting into a loan. A car losing its value ideally should not significantly impact your net worth.

I really regret buying Tesla

📺 "Driving Tesla's Cheapest Car | First Review of the 2026 Tesla Model 3 Standard"
by Edmunds Cars
📊 298,769 views | 1,841 likes | 285 comments  |  🏷️ review

⭐⭐⭐ EXECUTIVE SUMMARY ⭐⭐⭐
The 2026 Tesla Model 3 Standard is positioned as the cheapest car in Tesla's lineup, saving buyers over $5,000 compared to the Premium model. Despite a simpler suspension and a smaller battery, the vehicle retains its core driving dynamics, premium interior feel, and essential features like the panoramic glass roof. The reviewer concludes that the minimal compromises make the Standard model the default, logical choice for most buyers.

⭐⭐⭐ DETAILED BREAKDOWN ⭐⭐⭐
The video provides a comprehensive first drive review of the 2026 Tesla Model 3 Standard, the most affordable vehicle in Tesla's current lineup, priced around $38,630. Presenter Alistair Weaver questions whether this cheaper model suffers from aggressive cost-cutting, similar to what Edmunds observed in the Model Y Standard. 

Starting with the exterior and interior, the changes are minimal. The car features new aerodynamic wheel covers and subtle interior material swaps, like fabric replacing some vegan leather. Crucially, unlike the Model Y, the Model 3 Standard retains the panoramic glass roof and double-glazed front windows. While the rear infotainment screen has been removed—a change the presenter actually praises for family use—the cabin remains comfortable, well-appointed, and avoids feeling like a 'poverty spec' vehicle.

On the road, the Model 3 Standard features a less sophisticated suspension setup compared to the Premium model. However, because the sedan sits lower to the ground than an SUV, body roll is easily managed, resulting in a drive that still feels sporty, responsive, and traditionally Tesla. The smaller battery pack slightly reduces acceleration and range (claiming 321 miles), but the real-world performance remains punchy and more than adequate for daily driving.

Finally, the review touches on Tesla's autonomous driving software. A notable downgrade is that the standard Autopilot in this trim will no longer auto-steer on the highway unless the driver pays for the Full Self-Driving (FSD) upgrade—a move Weaver criticizes as a cynical marketing tactic. Despite this, the overall verdict is highly positive, declaring the Model 3 Standard as the smartest buy in the lineup and a formidable competitor against rivals like the Hyundai Ioniq 6 and Chevy Equinox EV.

⭐⭐⭐ KEY TAKEAWAYS ⭐⭐⭐
🎯 The Model 3 Standard retains premium features like the panoramic glass roof and front double-glazed windows, unlike the heavily de-contented Model Y Standard.
🎯 Despite a simpler suspension, the car's low center of gravity ensures it remains sporty, engaging, and limits body roll.
🎯 The rear infotainment screen has been removed and replaced with physical air vents and USB-C chargers.
🎯 Standard Autopilot on this model is software-limited and will not automatically steer on the highway unless the driver purchases the FSD upgrade.
🎯 At roughly $38,630, the minimal compromises make this trim the best value and default choice for most Model 3 buyers.

⭐⭐⭐ ACTIONABLE ADVICE ⭐⭐⭐
💡 Opt for the Model 3 Standard over the Premium version if you want to save $5,000 and do not require maximum range or track-level performance.
💡 Be aware that to get highway auto-steer functionality, you will need to pay an additional $99/month for the Full Self-Driving software.
💡 Use the frunk (front trunk) for versatile storage, as it remains fully functional and lined, unlike some downgraded models.

⭐⭐⭐ MEMORABLE QUOTES ⭐⭐⭐

text:
The Autopilot helped me eliminate Tesla from possible EV's I'll consider buying. I have a VW Alltrack with Adaptive Cruise Control very similar to Tesla cruise control, I also have Lane Assist.
I NEVER use Lane Assist for a few reasons namely the feedback thru the steering wheel it's like you're always fighting it, the car chooses where it wants to be in the lane and often it's too close to centerline like a 2 lane hwy (I prefer to drive over to the right in the lane, very often Lane Assist shuts down because it can't "see" the lines or there a gap in the road lines, Lane assist IMO is kind of unsafe (you cannot rely on it) so I never use it luckily unlike Tesla Autopilot I can shut off Lane Assist and still have Adaptive Cruise Control (which I Love) they're actually independent from each other  That's why I'd NEVER get a Tesla. Autopilot has merged 2 different functions and can not be separated not yet anyway maybe a software update could separate?
You didn't mention "PHANTOM BRAKING" (look it up) it's a major issue with Model 3 and Model Y and can be very dangerous the car can suddenly brake form any speed and come to a stop imagine that on a freeway...Phantom Braking happens when Autopilot is engaged! I can't help but wonder why Tesla integrated cruise control with autopilot...BIG mistake IMO. They lost me as a potential customer at least until they separate cruise control from lane assist so they're independent from each other.

text:
Usual warning, do not attempt this if you are not knowledgeable about high voltage and current wiring.
You should use at the very least a high quality outlet. Some say you should not use aluminum wiring. This is because it oxidizes. Using a quality socket like even the midrange Hubble outlet with proper cable clamps tightened to the required spec, very tight, you should be fine. Just monitor the outlet temp for the first few days after charging for an hour. Then check once a month for a year and once every year after that.
